source_text: Et poteram quidem omnium scripturarum caelestium euentilare tractatus, et ingentem circa istam speciem Christi diuinitatis, ut ita dixerim, siluam commouere: nisi quoniam non tam mihi contra hanc haeresim propositum est dicere, quam breuiter circa personam Christi regulam ueritatis aperire. quamuis tamen ad alia festinem, illud non arbitror praetermittendum, quod in euangelio dominus ad significantiam suae maiestatis expressit dicendo: soluite templum hoc, et ego in triduo suscitabo illud; aut quando in alio loco et alia parte pronuntiat: potestatem habeo animam meam ponendi et rursus recipere eam. hoc enim mandatum accepi a patre. quis est enim, qui dicit animam suam se posse ponere aut animam suam posse se rursum recuperare, quia hoc mandatum acceperit a patre? aut quis dicit destructum corporis sui templum resuscitare rursum et reaedificare se posse? nisi quoniam sermo ille, qui ex patre, qui apud patrem, per quem facta sunt omnia, et sine quo factum est nihil, imitator paternorum operum atque uirtutum, mago inuisibilis dei, qui descendit de caelo, qui quae uidit et audiuit testificatus est, qui non uenit ut faceret suam uoluntatem, sed potius ut faciat patris uoluntatem, a quo missus ad hoc ipsum fuerat, ut magni consilii angelus factus arcanorum caelestium nobis iura reseraret, quique uerbum caro factus habttauit in nobis, ex nobis hic Christus non homo tantum, quia hominis filius, sed etiam deus, quia dei filius, comprobatur. Quod si et primogenitus omnis creaturae ab apostolo dictus sit Christus, quomodo omnis creaturae primogenitus esse potuit, nisi quoniam secundum diuinitatem ante omnem creaturam ex patre deo sermo processit? quod nisi ita haeretici acceperint, Christum hominem primogenitum omnis creaturae monstrare cogentur; quod facere non poterunt. aut igitur ante omnem est creaturam, ut primogenitus sit omnis creaturae, et non homo est tantum, quia homo post omnem creaturam est: aut homo tantum est, et est post omnem creaturam. et quomodo primogenitus est omnis creaturae, nisi secundum uerbum illud quod est ante creaturam? et ideo primogenitus omnis creaturae caro fit et habitat in nobis, hoc est, assumit hunc hominem qui est post omnem creaturam, et sic cum illo et in illo habitat in nobis, ut neque homo Christo subtrahatur, neque diuinitas negetur. nam si tantummodo ante omnem creaturam est, homo in illo subtractus est. si autem tantummodo homo est, diuinitas quae ante omnem creaturam est intercepta est. utrumque ergo in Christo confoederatum est, et utrumque coniunctum est, et utrumque conexum est, et merito, dum est in illo aliquid quod superat creaturam, pignerata in illo diuinitatis et humanitatis uidetur esse concordia. propter quam causam, qui mediator dei et hominum effectus exprimitur, in se deum et hominem sociasse reperitur. Ac si idem apostolus de Christo refert, ut exutus carnem potestates dehonestauit, palam triumphatis illis in semetipso, non utique otiose exutum carne proposuit, nisi quoniam et in resurrectione rursum indutum uoluit intellegi. quis est ergo iste exutus et rursus indutus? requirant haeretici. nos enim sermonem dei scimus indutum carnis substantiam, eundemque rursum exutum eadem corporis materia, quam rursus in resurrectione suscepit et quasi indumentum resumpsit. sed enim neque exutus neque indutus hominem Christus fuisset, si homo tantum fuisset. nemo enim umquam se ipso aut spoliatur aut induitur. sit enim necesse est aliud, quicquid aliunde aut spoliatur aut induitur. ex quo merito sermo dei fuit, qui exutus est carnem et in resurrectione rursus indutus; exutus autem, quoniam et in natiuitate fuerat indutus. itaque in Christo deus est qui induitur, atque etiam exutus sit oportet: propterea quod is qui induitur, pariter et exuatur necesse est. induitur autem et exuitur homine, quasi quadam contexti corporis tunica. ac propterea consequenter sermo fuit, ut diximus, dei, qui modo indutus, modo exutus esse reperitur. hoc enim etiam in benedictionibus ante praedixit: Lauabit stolam suam in uino, et in sanguine uuae amictum suum. si stola in Christo caro est, et amictum ipsum corpus est, requiratur, quis est ille cuius corpus amictum est, et stola caro? nobis enim manifestum est carnem stolam et corpus amictum uerbi fuisse, qui uuae sanguine, id est uino, lauit substantiam corporis et materiam carnis, abluens ex parte suscepti hominis passione. ex quo siquidem lauatur, homo est, quia amictum, quod lauatur, caro est: qui autem lauat, uerbum dei est, qui ut lauaret amictum, amicti susceptor effectus est. merito ex ea substantia, quae recepta est ut lauaretur, homo exprimitur, sic ut ex uerbi auctoritate, qui lauit, deus esse monstretur.
pass_a_gloss: I could indeed have discussed all the heavenly scriptures and stirred up a great forest, so to speak, concerning the divinity of Christ, but since my purpose is not so much to speak against this heresy as to briefly open up the rule of truth concerning the person of Christ, although I am hurrying on to other things, I do not think it should be passed over that the Lord in the gospel expressed a sign of His majesty, saying: destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days; or when in another place and another part He pronounces: I have the power to lay down my soul and to take it up again, for I have received this command from the Father. Who is it that says he can lay down his soul or take it up again because he has received a command from the Father? Or who says that he can raise up and rebuild the destroyed temple of his body? Unless the Word, who is from the Father, who is with the Father, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, is the imitator of the Father's works and virtues, the messenger of the invisible God, who came down from heaven, who testified to what He saw and heard, who did not come to do His own will, but rather to do the will of the Father, who sent Him for this very purpose, so that as the angel of the great counsel He might reveal to us the mysteries of heaven, and who, having become flesh, dwelled among us, this Christ is proven to be not only human, because He is the son of man, but also God, because He is the son of God. But if Christ is called the firstborn of all creation by the apostle, how could He be the firstborn of all creation unless, according to His divinity, the Word proceeded from God the Father before all creation? Unless the heretics accept this, they will be forced to show that Christ, as a human, is the firstborn of all creation, which they cannot do. Therefore, either He is before all creation, so that He is the firstborn of all creation, and He is not only human, because human is after all creation; or He is only human, and He is after all creation. And how can He be the firstborn of all creation unless it is according to that Word which is before creation? And therefore, the firstborn of all creation becomes flesh and dwells among us, that is, He takes on this human who is after all creation, and thus He dwells among us with him and in him, so that neither the human is separated from Christ nor is the divinity denied. For if He is only before all creation, the human is separated from Him. But if He is only human, the divinity which is before all creation is intercepted. Therefore, both are united in Christ, and both are joined, and both are connected, and rightly so, since there is something in Him that surpasses creation, the concord of divinity and humanity seems to be pledged in Him. Because of this reason, He who is made the mediator of God and humans is found to have united God and human in Himself. And if the same apostle reports about Christ, that having stripped the flesh, He disgraced the powers, having triumphed over them in Himself, He did not propose to be stripped of flesh in vain, unless because He also wanted to be understood as having been clothed again in resurrection. Who is it, then, who is stripped and clothed again? Let the heretics ask. For we know that the Word of God was clothed with the substance of flesh and the same was stripped of the same material of the body, which He again took up in resurrection and, as it were, put on again as a garment. But if Christ had been only human, He would not have been stripped or clothed, for no one is ever stripped or clothed by himself. It must be something else, whatever is stripped or clothed from elsewhere. From which it follows that the Word of God was the one who was stripped of flesh and clothed again in resurrection; He was stripped because He had also been clothed in birth. And so in Christ, God is the one who is clothed, and it is necessary that He also be stripped; because the one who is clothed is also necessarily stripped. He is clothed and stripped, however, as a human, as if with a tunic of a woven body. And therefore, consequently, the Word was, as we said, of God, who is found to be clothed and stripped in turn. For He also predicted this in blessings beforehand: He will wash His robe in wine, and His garment in the blood of the grape. If the robe in Christ is flesh, and the garment is the body, let it be asked, who is it whose body is the garment, and whose flesh is the robe? For it is clear to us that the flesh is the robe and the body is the garment of the Word, who washed the substance of the body and the material of the flesh with the blood of the grape, that is, with wine, cleansing the passion of the assumed human. From which, if He is washed, He is human, because the garment that is washed is flesh; but He who washes is the Word of God, who, in order to wash the garment, became the receiver of the garment. Rightly, therefore, the human is expressed from the substance that was received to be washed, so that from the authority of the Word, who washed, God is shown to be.

pass_b_english: I could indeed have discussed every heavenly Scripture and stirred up a vast forest, so to speak, around this manifestation of Christ's divinity; yet my purpose is less to argue against this heresy than to set forth briefly the rule of truth concerning the person of Christ. Even as I hasten on to other matters, I do not think it right to pass over the fact that the Lord in the Gospel gave a sign of His majesty when He said, "Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days" (John 2:19); or when in another place He declared, "I have power to lay down my soul and to take it up again, for I have received this command from the Father" (John 10:18). Who could say he can lay down his own soul or take it up again simply because he received a command from the Father? Who could say he can raise up and rebuild the destroyed temple of his own body? Only the Word, who is from the Father, who was with the Father, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, the imitator of the Father's works and virtues, the messenger of the invisible God, who descended from heaven, who testified to what He saw and heard, who came not to do His own will but to do the will of the Father who sent Him for this very purpose — that as the Angel of the Great Counsel He might reveal to us the mysteries of heaven — and who, having become flesh, dwelt among us: this Christ is proved to be not only human, because He is the Son of Man, but also God, because He is the Son of God.

Now if the apostle calls Christ the firstborn of all creation, how could He be the firstborn of all creation unless, according to His divinity, the Word proceeded from God the Father before all creation? Unless the heretics accept this, they will be forced to show Christ as a human firstborn of all creation — something they cannot do. Either He is before all creation, so that He may be the firstborn of all creation, and is not merely human, because humanity comes after all creation; or He is only human, and thus comes after all creation. And how could He be the firstborn of all creation except according to that Word which is before creation? Therefore the firstborn of all creation becomes flesh and dwells in us — that is, He assumes this human who is after all creation, and thus He dwells in us with him and in him, so that neither is the human subtracted from Christ nor is the divinity denied. For if He is only before all creation, the human is subtracted from Him; but if He is only human, the divinity which is before all creation is cut off. Therefore both are united in Christ, both are joined, both are bound together; and rightly so, since there is something in Him that surpasses creation, the concord of divinity and humanity appears to be pledged in Him. For this reason He who is expressed as the mediator of God and humans is found to have united God and human in Himself.

And if the same apostle reports of Christ that, having stripped off the flesh, He disarmed the powers, triumphing over them in Himself, He did not propose the stripping of the flesh in vain, unless because He also wanted to be understood as clothed again in the resurrection. Who, then, is this one stripped and clothed again? Let the heretics ask. For we know that the Word of God was clothed with the substance of flesh, and the same Word was stripped of the same material of the body, which He took up again in the resurrection and, as it were, put on again as a garment. But if Christ had been only human, He would not have been stripped or clothed, for no one ever strips or clothes himself. There must be something else, whatever is stripped or clothed from elsewhere. It follows, then, that the Word of God was the one who was stripped of flesh and clothed again in the resurrection; He was stripped because He had also been clothed at His birth. So in Christ, God is the one who is clothed, and He must also be the one who is stripped; for the one who is clothed is necessarily also stripped. He is clothed and stripped, however, as a human, as with a tunic of a woven body. And therefore, consequently, the Word was, as we said, of God, who is found to be clothed and stripped in turn. For He also foretold this in blessings beforehand: "He will wash His robe in wine, and His garment in the blood of the grape." If the robe in Christ is flesh, and the garment is the body, let it be asked: who is He whose body is the garment, and whose flesh is the robe? For it is clear to us that the flesh was the robe and the body the garment of the Word, who washed the substance of the body and the material of the flesh with the blood of the grape — that is, with wine — cleansing the passion of the assumed human. From this it follows: if He is washed, He is human, because the garment that is washed is flesh; but He who washes is the Word of God, who, in order to wash the garment, became the receiver of the garment. Rightly, therefore, the human is expressed from the substance that was received to be washed, so that from the authority of the Word who washed, God is shown to be.
